strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem: predicting answer failure before generation. A lightweight probe on frozen representations offers a practical alternative to full fine-tuning, supported by the efficiency measurements in Table 2.

Table 1 establishes useful predictive signal. The default probe achieves 85.0–88.7% AUROC on PopQA/Entity Questions and 68.9–71.4% on Natural Questions, with performance generally competitive with or better than the fine-tuning baseline.

Figure 5 provides promising empirical evidence for transfer: adaptation consistently improves over directly applying a source-model probe, often approaching supervised target-model performance. Appendix I additionally examines transfer involving Gemma and different representation dimensions.

The experiments include useful ablations of token pooling, layers, training-set size, kernels, and question-aligned batches. The matched-size comparison and explicit discussion of weaker Natural Questions performance help characterize the method’s limitations.
weaknesses: The central inference about shared conditional distributions is unsupported. In Section 5.1, comparable pooled-versus-individual AUROC does not establish equal P(y|X): AUROC measures ranking, and a pooled MLP can implement different rules in distinguishable model-specific feature regions. Agreement between fitted predictors likewise does not identify the underlying conditional distributions. The experiments support successful adaptation, but do not demonstrate the claimed absence of concept shift.

Equation 7 states a strict improvement in distribution-distance estimation without assumptions or proof; aligned batches need not produce a smaller estimation error for every draw. Figure 6 supports their empirical usefulness, not this general inequality. Similarly, better results with linear-kernel MMD, which matches feature means, do not establish that the features are inherently discriminative.

Label validity is only partially established. Exact substring matching can reject correct alternative expressions and accept responses that mention the gold answer while contradicting it. The manual audit covers only 180 automatically negative/factual examples, leaving the claim that all positive/non-factual examples are correctly labeled unverified. Including abstentions is consistent with the stated task, but the resulting evidence concerns short-answer success and should not be generalized to factuality without qualification.

Important controls are missing. The closest question-representation probing method [18] is discussed but not evaluated, and there is no linear probe trained on the same correctness labels. For transfer, training directly on target representations using paired source-model labels would be a particularly informative baseline. Evaluating questions where source and target correctness disagree would also help distinguish model-specific transfer from shared question difficulty.

Reproducibility and evaluation selection remain insufficiently specified. The answer-generation prompts, exact extraction position relative to chat-template tokens, fixed splits, and random seeds are not supplied. Most critically, the paper does not explain how adaptation checkpoints and kernels are selected without target labels, although target-test learning curves are presented. Repeated-run uncertainty is also absent. These gaps, together with the unsupported invariance argument, prevent a clear Findings recommendation despite the promising empirical core.
